claim: Bioluminescence is used by a diverse set of organisms to achieve goals such as attracting mates, scaring off predators and recruiting other creatures to spread spores.
source: Bioluminescence is used by a diverse set of organisms to achieve a broad range of goals, such as attracting mates, scaring off predators and recruiting other creatures to spread spores (Shimomura, 2006; Wainwright and Longo, 2017; Verdes and Gruber, 2017; Labella et al., 2017; Oliveira et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The mechanism of light emission in bioluminescence is broadly conserved: an enzymatic oxidation reaction by a luciferase enzyme turns a luciferin substrate into a high energy intermediate, which decays to produce light.
source: The mechanism of light emission is broadly conserved: an enzymatic oxidation reaction by a luciferase enzyme turns a luciferin substrate into a high energy intermediate, which decays to produce light (Shimomura, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Several different luciferin substrate-luciferase enzyme pairs have been described to date.
source: Several different luciferin substrate-luciferase enzyme pairs have been described to date (Oba et al., 2017; Schultz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Firefly and Renilla luciferases have been leveraged to build reporters to study gene expression in plants and other eukaryotic systems.
source: Researchers have leveraged some enzymes, such as the firefly and Renilla luciferases, to build reporters to study gene expression in plants and other eukaryotic systems (Khakhar et al., 2018; Wend et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Bioluminescent reporters have a high signal to noise ratio because plants produce effectively no background bioluminescence signal.
source: These reporters have a high signal to noise ratio because plants produce effectively no background bioluminescence signal.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about plant biology and bioluminescence

claim: Firefly luciferase can be used to visualize dynamic changes in gene expression in plants in a non-invasive manner, theoretically enabling whole-plant time lapse imaging.
source: Additionally, thanks to its water-soluble luciferin substrate, firefly luciferase can be used to visualize dynamic changes in gene expression in plants in a non-invasive manner, theoretically enabling whole-plant time lapse imaging (Khakhar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Uniform delivery and penetration of the luciferin substrate is a major challenge, especially in adult plant tissues.
source: One major challenge is uniform delivery and penetration of the luciferin substrate, especially in adult plant tissues.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about substrate delivery challenges

claim: Coelenterazine, the substrate for Renilla luciferase, is non-water soluble and cannot be used for imaging without cell-lysis.
source: Some luciferins, such as coelenterazine – the substrate for Renilla luciferase – are non-water soluble and cannot be used for imaging without cell-lysis (Wend et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: D-luciferin for firefly luciferase is water soluble and can be topically applied to whole plants or delivered through watering.
source: The luciferin for firefly luciferase, D-luciferin, is water soluble and can be topically applied to whole plants or delivered through watering (Rellán-Álvarez et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Uniform substrate delivery is challenging to achieve, making it difficult to disambiguate whether an absence of bioluminescent signal is due to low luciferase expression or poor substrate delivery.
source: However, uniform substrate delivery is challenging to achieve, making it difficult to disambiguate whether an absence of bioluminescent signal is due to low luciferase expression or poor substrate delivery.
evidence: Based on logical inference from substrate delivery challenges

claim: D-luciferin has a relatively high cost of up to several hundred dollars per gram.
source: Additionally, the relatively high cost of D-luciferin (up to several hundred dollars per gram) makes continuous whole-plant imaging a prohibitively expensive practice.
evidence: Based on knowledge of commercial substrate costs

claim: Krichevsky et al. demonstrated an approach to achieve substrate-independent bioluminescence by incorporating the lux operon from Photobacterium leiognathi into the chloroplast genome in Nicotiana tabacum.
source: Krichevsky et al. demonstrated one approach to achieve this by incorporating the lux operon from the prokaryote Photobacterium leiognathi into the chloroplast genome in Nicotiana tabacum (Krichevsky et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Auto-luminescence was observed in tobacco plants with the lux operon incorporated into the chloroplast genome.
source: While auto-luminescence was observed, this approach is extremely challenging to extend to other plants due to the technical challenges of plastid transformation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Krichevsky et al., 2010

claim: Plastid localization is necessary for the lux operon approach because the luciferin substrate produced by this pathway is toxic in some eukaryotic systems when nuclearly encoded.
source: Plastid localization is necessary, as the luciferin substrate produced by this pathway is toxic in some eukaryotic systems when nuclearly encoded (Hollis et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Kotlobay et al. identified a fungal bioluminescence pathway consisting of three genes sufficient to convert caffeic acid into a luciferin molecule.
source: In their 2018 paper, Kotlobay et al. identified a fungal bioluminescence pathway (FBP) consisting of a set of three genes sufficient to convert caffeic acid, a common plant metabolite (Kotlobay et al., 2018), into a luciferin molecule.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Caffeic acid is a common plant metabolite.
source: In their 2018 paper, Kotlobay et al. identified a fungal bioluminescence pathway (FBP) consisting of a set of three genes sufficient to convert caffeic acid, a common plant metabolite (Kotlobay et al., 2018), into a luciferin molecule.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The fungal luciferase Luz can oxidize the luciferin and generate a bioluminescent signal.
source: The paired luciferase, Luz, can oxidize the luciferin and generate a bioluminescent signal (Kotlobay et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway can be nuclearly encoded, overcoming the challenges associated with plastid transformation.
source: This pathway can be nuclearly encoded, overcoming the challenges associated with plastid transformation.
evidence: Based on inference from the properties of the fungal pathway

claim: The fungal luciferase produces light in the green spectrum, which minimizes absorption by chlorophyll.
source: Additionally, the luciferase produces light in the green spectrum, which minimizes absorption by the predominant plant pigment, chlorophyll (Kaskova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The fungal luciferase is spectrally separable from firefly luciferase, enabling parallel deployment of both reporters.
source: This also makes it spectrally separable from the other major luciferase-based reporters, such as firefly luciferase, enabling the parallel deployment of both these reporters (Kaskova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway was successfully reconstituted in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves through transient expression.
source: When N. benthamiana leaves were imaged three days after delivery of the FBP via Agrobacterium infiltration, significant bioluminescence was observed over background at the site of infiltration (Figure 1B,C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway can produce bioluminescence using natively synthesized caffeic acid.
source: This demonstrates the pathway can produce bioluminescence using natively synthesized caffeic acid.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results showing bioluminescence without external substrate

claim: Bioluminescence signal was only observed with the complete fungal bioluminescence pathway, not with controls missing pathway enzymes.
source: Comparing luminescence from leaves with the complete pathway versus controls with missing pathway enzymes, a bioluminescence signal was only observed with the complete pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: No native enzymes are expressed at functional levels in N. benthamiana leaves that could complement the functions of the FBP enzymes absent in incomplete pathways.
source: This indicates no native enzymes are expressed at functional levels in N. benthamiana leaves that could complement the functions of the FBP enzymes absent in these incomplete pathways.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results with incomplete pathways

claim: No bioluminescence was observed from confluent cultures of Agrobacterium carrying the pathway.
source: We also observed no bioluminescence from confluent cultures of Agrobacterium carrying the pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), implying the observed bioluminescent signal was not from expression of this pathway in Agrobacterium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Incorporating the caffeylpyruvate hydrolase (CPH) enzyme into the reconstituted pathway creates a recycling pathway that converts spent luciferin back to caffeic acid.
source: In their paper, (Kotlobay et al., 2018). also describe an additional enzyme, caffeylpyruvate hydrolase (CPH), which recycles the spent luciferin, caffeylpyruvic acid, back to the substrate for the pathway, caffeic acid (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and shown in figure

claim: At later time points (7 days post-infiltration), higher mean luminescence signal was observed from leaves infiltrated with the CPH-containing pathway compared to pathways without CPH.
source: At later time points we saw higher mean luminescence signal from leaves infiltrated with the CPH containing pathway, consistent with the hypothesis that when the substrate is limited, the presence of a recycling pathway improves the bioluminescence signal (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: At four days post-infiltration, approximately equal luminescence signals were observed between pathways with and without CPH.
source: When we compared luminescence from Agrobacterium infiltrated N. benthamiana leaves, we observed approximately equal signals at four days, consistent with initial saturating substrate conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Stable transgenic lines of N. benthamiana expressing the fungal bioluminescence pathway exhibit auto-luminescence throughout the plant.
source: When luminescence was characterized in plants on rooting medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) or soil (Figure 1F,G, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B), we observed auto-luminescence throughout the plant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Stronger bioluminescence signals were observed in the root tips and shoot apical meristem of stable transgenic N. benthamiana plants.
source: Stronger signals were observed in the root tips and shoot apical meristem, consistent with a higher density of cells in these tissues.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and inference about cell density

claim: Younger leaves have lower luminescence than older leaves in stable transgenic N. benthamiana plants expressing the fungal bioluminescence pathway.
source: Younger leaves also seemed to have lower luminescence than older leaves, indicating there is some developmentally consistent heterogeneity in luciferin substrate biosynthesis, potentially due to variation in caffeic acid availability (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in figures

claim: Expression of a caffeic acid biosynthesis pathway increases luminescence in stable transgenic N. benthamiana lines expressing the fungal bioluminescence pathway.
source: Upon infiltration of this construct into leaves of a N. benthamiana line stably expressing the FBP, a significant increase in bioluminescence signal was observed compared to empty vector controls infiltrated in parallel on different sections of the same leaf (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The caffeic acid biosynthesis pathway consists of Rhodobacter capsulatus tyrosine ammonia lyase and two Escherichia coli 4-hydroxyphenylacetate 3-monooxygenase components (HpaB, HpaC) that catalyze caffeic acid synthesis from tyrosine.
source: To test this, we built a T-DNA to constitutively express the Rhodobacter capsulatus tyrosine ammonia lyase and two Escherichia coli 4-hydroxyphenylacetate 3-monooxygenase components (HpaB, HpaC). Together these enzymes are known to catalyze caffeic acid synthesis from tyrosine (Kotlobay et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Caffeic acid is ubiquitous in higher plants.
source: While N. benthamiana is an excellent model for prototyping, FBP should work in any plant species as long as appropriate promoters and terminators are used to express the pathway enzymes and as caffeic acid is ubiquitous in higher plants (Davin and Lewis, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway functions in Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings.
source: We performed transient Agrobacterium-based delivery of the FBP into the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana and the crop plant Solanum lycopersicum (tomato) (Wu et al., 2014). We observed robust auto-luminescence signal over background in the cotyledons of treated seedlings (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway functions in Solanum lycopersicum (tomato) seedlings.
source: We performed transient Agrobacterium-based delivery of the FBP into the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana and the crop plant Solanum lycopersicum (tomato) (Wu et al., 2014). We observed robust auto-luminescence signal over background in the cotyledons of treated seedlings (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway functions in Dahlia leaves.
source: We also performed Agrobacterium infiltrations of the leaves of the ornamental plant, Dahlia, and again observed auto-luminescence (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway is functional in petals of Catharanthus roseus (periwinkle).
source: Agrobacterium infiltrations with the FBP of petals from Catharanthus roseus (periwinkle), Petunia hybrida, and three different varieties of Rosa rubiginosa (Rose) resulted in auto-luminescence in all flowers with a range of intensities (Figure 2D,E, Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway is functional in petals of Petunia hybrida.
source: Agrobacterium infiltrations with the FBP of petals from Catharanthus roseus (periwinkle), Petunia hybrida, and three different varieties of Rosa rubiginosa (Rose) resulted in auto-luminescence in all flowers with a range of intensities (Figure 2D,E, Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway is functional in petals of three different varieties of Rosa rubiginosa (Rose).
source: Agrobacterium infiltrations with the FBP of petals from Catharanthus roseus (periwinkle), Petunia hybrida, and three different varieties of Rosa rubiginosa (Rose) resulted in auto-luminescence in all flowers with a range of intensities (Figure 2D,E, Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The bioluminescence signal dropped off within a day of flowers being detached from the plant body, whereas it persisted when flowers remained connected to the plant body.
source: We also observed that the signal dropped off within a day of the flowers being detached from the plant body, whereas it persisted when the flowers remained connected to the plant body.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Some of the pathway substrates or co-factors may be trafficked from source tissues.
source: This might mean some of the pathway substrates or co-factors are trafficked from source tissues; however, more tests are required to confirm this hypothesis.
evidence: Speculative inference from experimental observations

claim: The ODO1 gene from petunia has been previously characterized with a firefly luciferase reporter, where its expression was observed only in flowers.
source: This gene has been previously characterized in petunia with a firefly luciferase reporter, where its expression was observed only in the flowers.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fenske et al., 2015

claim: ODO1 expression is diurnal, peaking in the evening at the transition of day to night.
source: ODO1 expression was also shown to be diurnal, peaking in the evening at the transition of day to night (Fenske et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In petunia flowers treated with pODO1:Luz, an increase in luminescence was observed in the evening at the transition between day and night.
source: In the flowers treated with the pODO1:Luz we observed an increase in luminescence in the evening at the transition between day and night, a trend not seen in the 35S:Luz control (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The luminescence signal from pODO1:Luz constructs peaks around the expected time at the transition of day to night, in contrast to p35S controls.
source: When we plot the time at which we observe peak luminescence signal in these time course experiments, we observe that the signal from the pODO1:Luz constructs peak around the expected time, at the transition of day to night, in contrast to the p35S controls, which do not (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: At two days post infiltration, there is a significant difference between the time of peak signal of pODO1:Luz and the p35S:Luz control.
source: At 1 day post infiltration this trend is visible but not significant, potentially due to the initial variability in Agrobacterium delivery and associated expression of the delivered genes, but by two days post infection we see a significant difference between the time of peak signal of pODO1:Luz and the control (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures with statistical analysis

claim: The observed diurnal oscillations in pODO1:Luz are not due to natural variation in the availability of caffeic acid.
source: This difference in the temporal pattern of luminescence between pODO1:Luz and p35S:Luz indicates that the observed diurnal oscillations are not due to natural variation in the availability of caffeic acid, and highlights the importance of running parallel constitutive promoter controls for proper interpretation of FBP reporters.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental comparison with constitutive promoter control

claim: The AtRAB18 promoter has been previously characterized as driving a strong and selective expression increase in response to the plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA).
source: This promoter has previously been characterized as driving a strong and selective expression increase in response to the plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The fungal bioluminescence pathway with pRAB18-driven Luz reports ABA levels in a dose-dependent manner in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: To do this, we assayed the bioluminescent signal produced three days after infiltration into N. benthamiana leaves that were treated with increasing concentrations of ABA. As expected, we observed increasing bioluminescence signal with increasing doses of ABA (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The sensitivity of the pRAB18 driven FBP reporter is consistent with the previously characterized pRAB18 driven GFP reporter, as both are responsive to 10 µM ABA.
source: The sensitivity of the pRAB18 driven FBP reporter was consistent with the previously characterized pRAB18 driven GFP reporter, as both were responsive to 10 µM ABA (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by comparison with published literature and experimental data

claim: A significant increase in luminescence was observed in desiccating N. benthamiana leaves infiltrated with pRAB18-driven FBP.
source: In fact, we observed a significant increase in luminescence in desiccating leaves, up to levels of the unwatered p35S:Luz positive control (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: No similar increase in signal was observed from pRAB18 driven FBP in leaves that were kept moist.
source: We did not see a similar increase in signal from pRAB18 driven FBP in leaves that were kept moist (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: An increase in luminescence was observed in the leaf infiltrated with pRAB18 driven FBP on the unwatered plant over time, as compared to the watered plant control.
source: We repeated the experiment without detaching the infiltrated leaves from the plant body and again observed an increase in luminescence in the leaf infiltrated with pRAB18 driven FBP on the unwatered plant over time, as compared to the watered plant control, which showed no increase in luminescence (Figure 4D, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and video

claim: Luminescence from the p35S:Luz control remained similar for the watered and un-watered conditions.
source: Luminescence from the p35S:Luz control remained similar for the watered and un-watered conditions (Figure 4D, Figure 4—video 1), demonstrating that the dynamics visualized by the pRAB18:Luz reporter are not due to variation in caffeic acid levels or differential expression patterns of other promoters in the pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and video

claim: The dynamics visualized by the pRAB18:Luz reporter are not due to variation in caffeic acid levels or differential expression patterns of other promoters in the pathway.
source: Luminescence from the p35S:Luz control remained similar for the watered and un-watered conditions (Figure 4D, Figure 4—video 1), demonstrating that the dynamics visualized by the pRAB18:Luz reporter are not due to variation in caffeic acid levels or differential expression patterns of other promoters in the pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental comparison with constitutive promoter control

claim: Commercial bioluminescence imaging systems can exceed $100,000 USD.
source: However, the high cost and small chamber size of commercially available luminescence imaging setups make running multiple experiments in parallel cost prohibitive: such commercial systems can exceed $100,000 USD.
evidence: Based on knowledge of commercial equipment costs

claim: A low-cost bioluminescence imaging platform was developed using a Raspberry Pi, DSLR camera, and off-the-shelf components for less than $2,500.
source: Our platform uses a Raspberry Pi single board computer as a controller for a DSLR camera, outfitted with a macro lens and mounted in either a dark room or pop-up plant growth tent. The code used for controlling customized still and time-course imaging with this platform, as well as the image processing pipeline, is available on Github (Table 2). The entire cost comes to less than $2,500, the bulk of which is for the camera and lens; substituting an entry-level DSLR and kit lens would bring the cost below $2000.
evidence: Supported by experimental implementation and cost data in Table 2

claim: The DSLR-based imaging platform provides sufficient sensitivity to capture the bioluminescence signal from stable or transient expression of the FBP.
source: With programmatically controlled long exposures and a tripod stabilizer, the DSLR camera provides high resolution and detail for macroscopic plant subjects under multiple light conditions, and sufficient sensitivity to capture the bioluminescence signal from stable or transient expression of the FBP.
evidence: Supported by experimental demonstration of the platform

claim: Higher levels of thermodynamic noise are observed with the DSLR-based system than with cooled CCD camera setups, but this is easily filtered using open-source software such as ImageJ.
source: We do observe higher levels of thermodynamic noise than with cooled CCD camera setups, but this is easily filtered using open-source software such as ImageJ (Schindelin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citation to software

claim: Incorporating the recycling pathway prolongs the luminescent signal, suggesting an avenue to enable long term imaging without substrate depletion in stable lines.
source: Our observation that incorporating the recycling pathway prolongs the luminescent signal suggests an avenue to enable long term imaging without substrate depletion in stable lines.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: Stronger luminescence observed in infiltrated tissue than in stable transgenic lines might be due to overexpression of the enzymes from high-copy delivery of the T-DNAs in transient leaf infiltration assays.
source: This may also explain why we observed stronger luminescence in infiltrated tissue than in the stable transgenic line. However, this might also be due to overexpression of the enzymes from high-copy delivery of the T-DNAs in our transient leaf infiltration assay.
evidence: Speculative inference from experimental observations

claim: The fungal luciferase emits in the green spectrum and should be spectrally separable from firefly luciferase, permitting parallel deployment.
source: Because it emits in the green spectrum (Kaskova et al., 2017), Luz should be spectrally separable from firefly luciferase, permitting parallel deployment.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and inference about parallel use

claim: The FBP-based biosensors and reporters can be extended across a range of plants for long term visualization of gene expression using rapid morphogen-mediated plant transgenesis protocols.
source: With the recent development of rapid morphogen-mediated plant transgenesis protocols (Lowe et al., 2018), we believe FBP-based biosensors and reporters can be extended across a range of plants for long term visualization of gene expression.
evidence: Based on inference from recent developments in plant transgenesis and citation

claim: The FBP approach to auto-luminescence is superior to the existing transplastomic approach because plastid transformation is technically challenging and currently limited to species such as tobacco and a few related Solanaceae.
source: This extensibility to a broad range of plants makes this approach to auto-luminescence superior to the existing transplastomic approach (Krichevsky et al., 2010), as plastid transformation is technically challenging and currently limited to species such as tobacco and a few related Solanaceae (Rigano et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and inference

claim: The FBP can be used to study the spatiotemporal patterns of gene expression, reporting the same patterns as a firefly luciferase reporter but without the requirement for substrate addition.
source: Our results with the pODO1 driven Luz in petunia flowers demonstrate how the FBP can be used to study the spatiotemporal patterns of gene expression, reporting the same patterns of gene expression as a firefly luciferase reporter (Fenske et al., 2015), but without the requirement for substrate addition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to published literature

claim: A lower amplitude response is observed with FBP reporters compared to previously published luciferase reporters that are provided an excess of substrate during application.
source: Compared to these previously published luciferase reporters, which are typically provided an excess of substrate during application, we observe a lower amplitude response with our FBP reporters, which rely on an endogenously synthesized luciferin substrate.
evidence: Based on comparison with published literature and experimental observations

claim: FBP reporters can be used to visualize changes in gene expression that occur on the timescale of hours.
source: However, the data presented here do show that our FBP reporters can be used to visualize changes in gene expression that occur on the timescale of hours.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: In its natural context, the FBP is used by fungi to generate luminescence to lure insects that spread their spores.
source: In its natural context, the FBP is used by fungi to generate luminescence to lure insects that spread their spores (Oliveira et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: It may be possible to engineer plants with sufficiently bright auto-luminescent flowers to attract nocturnal insects and thereby drive novel plant-pollinator interactions.
source: It may then be possible to engineer plants with sufficiently bright auto-luminescent flowers to attract nocturnal insects, and thereby drive novel plant-pollinator interactions.
evidence: Speculative inference about future applications

claim: Bioluminescent flowers would have relevance for designer floriculture and might serve as a visually compelling demonstration of the power of synthetic biology to the public.
source: Bioluminescent flowers would also have relevance for designer floriculture, and might serve as a visually compelling demonstration of the power of synthetic biology to the public.
evidence: Speculative inference about future applications

claim: Stable FBP lines could be deployed to monitor the environmental impact on plants at field scales.
source: In the future, stable lines generated with similar constructs could be deployed to monitor the environmental impact on plants at field scales.
evidence: Speculative inference about future applications

claim: FBP biosensors would have an output more easily visualized than fluorescent reporters, have a high signal to noise ratio, and be cost effective due to their substrate independence.
source: These biosensors would have an output more easily visualized than fluorescent reporters, have a high signal to noise ratio, and be cost effective due to their substrate independence.
evidence: Based on inference from the properties of the FBP system

claim: The FBP approach could be easily extended to build biosensors for a range of different phytohormones, environmental cues like light, or synthetic signaling systems.
source: Thanks to the ease of promoter swapping in our FBP toolkit, this approach could be easily extended to build biosensors for a range of different phytohormones, environmental cues like light, or synthetic signaling systems for basic science and translational applications.
evidence: Based on inference from the modular design of the toolkit

claim: Caffeic acid is a requisite intermediate of lignin biosynthesis.
source: Caffeic acid is a requisite intermediate of lignin biosynthesis and is thus ubiquitous in higher plants (Davin and Lewis, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Caffeic acid levels may vary between tissues and under different environmental conditions.
source: However, caffeic acid levels may vary between tissues and under different environmental conditions (Mitiouchkina et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Codon-optimized versions of NPGA, H3H, Hisps, and Luz were synthesized for expression in plants.
source: We synthesized codon-optimized versions of the three genes necessary to convert caffeic acid into 3-hydroxyhispidin: 4′-phosphopantetheinyl transferase (NPGA) from Aspergillus nidulans, hispidin-3-hydroxylase (H3H) from Neonothopanus nambi, and a polyketide synthase (Hisps) also from N. nambi (Kotlobay et al., 2018; Figure 1A). We also generated a codon optimized version of the fungal luciferase, Luz.
evidence: Supported by experimental methods and citation

claim: The DNA sequences for FBP components were domesticated to remove commonly used type II-S restriction enzyme recognition sites and made compatible with the MoClo plasmid assembly kit.
source: These DNA sequences were domesticated to remove commonly used type II-S restriction enzyme recognition sites, and made compatible with the MoClo plasmid assembly kit (Engler et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental methods and citation

claim: The MoClo plasmid assembly kit enables rapid swapping of promoters and terminators to create custom expression cassettes.
source: This kit enables rapid swapping of promoters and terminators to create custom expression cassettes, which can be easily assembled into a single T-DNA with a one-step GoldenGate reaction.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the MoClo system

claim: The new FBP components comprise a toolbox of vectors to construct FBPs for constitutive or spatio-temporally regulated auto-luminescence.
source: Together, our new components comprise a toolbox of vectors to construct FBPs for constitutive or spatio-temporally regulated auto-luminescence (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental development of the toolkit

claim: Caffeic acid produced by the phenylpropanoid biosynthesis pathway is converted to Hispidin by Hisps once it is post-translationally activated by NPGA.
source: Caffeic acid produced by the phenylpropanoid biosynthesis pathway is converted to Hispidin by Hisps once it is post-translationally activated by NPGA.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A schematic and based on published pathway

claim: Hispidin is converted to 3-Hydroxyhispidin, the luciferin molecule, by H3H.
source: Hispidin is then converted to 3-Hydroxyhispidin, the luciferin molecule, by H3H.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A schematic and based on published pathway

claim: The luciferase Luz oxidizes 3-Hydroxyhispidin to a high energy intermediate which degrades into Caffeylpyruvic acid, producing light.
source: Finally, the luciferase Luz oxidizes 3-Hydroxyhispidin to a high energy intermediate which degrades into Caffeylpyruvic acid, producing light.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A schematic and based on published pathway

claim: CPH can turn Caffeylpyruvic acid back into Caffeic acid, closing the cycle.
source: CPH can turn Caffeylpyruvic acid back into Caffeic acid, closing the cycle.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A schematic and based on published pathway
